dimensions.name: Reference mining & contract inference

evidence.note: Reads both fixture next-shims.d.ts files early, explicitly to 'understand the full API surface' — grounding shims in actual type signatures rather than memory.

While writing shims, repeatedly reads next-source implementations matching each subsystem (navigation.ts for useRouter/usePathname, headers.ts/cookies.ts, after.ts, connection.ts, web exports, base-server), tying each next/* shim to a real contract.

Re-consults @vitejs/plugin-rsc internals (getEntrySource, environments, rollupOptions) and README multiple times to resolve ambiguous RSC/Vite-plugin integration semantics rather than guessing — level-8 behavior.

No further reference reads for the remaining ~100 steps; work becomes test-infra debugging (npx/npm/playwright) and feature edits by assertion (e.g. hydration approach inferred from test behavior at step 244), so grounding is not sustained throughout the build.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent's research phase strongly matches the level-8 anchor: it systematically mapped vendored Next.js source and Vite/plugin-rsc hooks to the required subsystems, extracted contracts from both fixture shims, re-consulted plugin-rsc source when RSC integration was ambiguous, and noted non-obvious semantics (hydration keys, headers/cookies context). It falls short of a full 8/10 because grounding was heavily front-loaded and collapsed after step 167 into infrastructure debugging and assertion-driven feature edits, so reference mining was not sustained across the whole horizon — placing it solidly between the 5 and 8 anchors at 7.

dimensions.name: Subsystem decomposition & sequencing

evidence.note: First real decomposition is a flat list mirroring requirement bullets — 'package.json+bin, source TS, Vite plugin resolving next/* + SSR, CLI commands, shims' — with no dependency ordering or per-milestone done-criteria. Plan is 'build the complete vinext package' (big-bang), not a minimal vertical slice.

Only place a sensible ordered sub-sequence appears: study routing → implement route resolution → SSR rendering → both routers/middleware. Shows major subsystems identified and a reasonable order (resolution/plugin before routing before SSR), matching the lower half of anchor 5, but still coarse and not tied to specific fixtures/tests.

Long undifferentiated exploration with ~60 near-identical 'examine reference, then start building the scaffold' plans; no distinction of independently-verifiable subsystems or milestone boundaries emerges from this phase.

The bulk of the horizon is undifferentiated firefighting (terminal hangs, npm offline, node_modules symlinks, Playwright resolution) with repetitive '1. fix CLI 2. rerun tests' plans. No milestone was ever declared 'done' via a passing test subset, and boundaries were never re-planned as coupling surfaced — the through-line is a single big-bang push, not sequenced slices.
Task submitted after only being able to LIST 341 tests; no evidence of a milestone-gated end-to-end path ever being proven by tests, confirming absence of test-anchored done-criteria.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent identified the major subsystems (shim/resolution, dev server, routing, SSR, middleware, config, CLI) and at a couple of points picked a sensible dependency-respecting order (resolution/plugin → routing → SSR), with only a rough notion of 'done' ('dev server starts', 'SSR works') — the hallmarks of anchor 5. But its actual plans were overwhelmingly flat lists mirroring the requirement bullets (anchor 3), it pursued a big-bang implementation rather than a minimal verifiable vertical slice, and it never tied milestones to concrete fixtures/tests or re-planned boundaries as coupling emerged. This lands between the flat-list (3) and clean-subsystem-ordering (5) anchors, at 4.

dimensions.name: Test-driven verification design

evidence.note: Read many spec files (ssr, headers-cookies, routes, navigation, advanced) to understand test expectations before/while implementing — input to verification design.

Ran full run_tests.sh ~24 times as the primary correctness oracle, but never obtained actual pass/fail counts (results file never produced); used it as a coarse all-or-nothing gate rather than a targeted debugger.

Stood up fixture apps manually in /tmp and ran `vinext dev -p PORT` to reproduce and debug dev-server startup failures, using errors to guide fixes — fixture-level verification, but confined to 'does it boot' rather than behavior.
Built a 'PIPE simulation' probe to reproduce the stderr pipe-buffer deadlock the test runner triggers — a real targeted probe, still at the infrastructure layer.

Ended by re-running the full suite and self-declaring completeness from a feature checklist; never ran targeted subsets, never curled manual servers to verify SSR/SSG/action output, never tested the production build/start path.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent went beyond a pure code-only assumption and beyond a bare oracle: it read specs, stood up individual fixtures manually, and devised targeted infrastructure probes (dev-server boot tests, PIPE-deadlock simulation), using failures to drive fixes (above anchor 3). But it never ran targeted test subsets, its behavioral verification never advanced past 'server starts / basic HTML' (no HTTP probes of SSR/SSG/action output), the suite never actually reported pass/fail to guide it, and the production build/start paths were never verified — all required for anchor 5. This places it at a 4, between the oracle-only and subset-driven anchors.

dimensions.name: Progress & pass-rate tracking across subsystems

evidence.note: First full test run: dev servers failed to start, no pass/fail data obtained. Agent immediately pivots to debugging infrastructure rather than establishing any baseline pass count.

Dozens of consecutive run_tests.sh invocations all blocked on the same class of failures (dev server startup, symlinks, npx vinext). Agent loops on the same infrastructure failure; at step 178 it does step back to 'replicate test runner steps manually,' a partial loop-break, but never reaches test results.

Repeated checks of /tmp/playwright-env-results.json which is never created ('no results file'). Agent keeps stating intent to 'get a baseline, then systematically improve' but never obtains any pass count or per-subsystem pass-rate.

Progress is tracked only as a static list of features it believes it implemented (CLI, shims, routing, SSR, etc.), not as tested pass-rate by area — a feature-built recollection, not evidence-based done-vs-remaining.
Declares task complete three times with zero test-pass evidence, citing only that Playwright 'can list 341 tests.' Demonstrates an inaccurate, unfounded model of what actually passes vs. remains.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent kept a vague, feature-list recollection of progress and reacted to whichever infrastructure failure was in front of it, but never once obtained a pass/fail count or tracked pass-rate by subsystem against real test evidence — the results file was never populated across ~20 runs. It looped extensively on the same startup/resolution failures and ultimately declared success with no test evidence, indicating an inaccurate done-vs-remaining picture. This matches anchor 3 (vague recollection, notices only the failure in front of it), sitting just above pure reactivity due to a feature checklist and occasional loop-breaking, and clearly short of anchor 5's evidence-based pass-count tracking.

dimensions.name: Design revision under divergence

evidence.note: Falsified assumption that `npm install` downloads deps (no internet) drove a real revision of the packaging approach: dependencies → peerDependencies + offline config + runtime symlinks. Approach-level rework, not just a patch.

When @vitejs/plugin-rsc demanded build.rollupOptions.input, the agent explicitly weighed 'configure environments properly OR implement our own SSR middleware' and pivoted to disabling serverHandler + own middleware. Deliberate — but a bypass of the RSC foundation rather than wiring it correctly, which undercuts later subsystems (use cache/RSC).

Long stretch of local fixes (symlinks, stderr pipe deadlock, ESM/CJS require, npx resolution) to the runtime node_modules foundation — repeated patching without revisiting whether the hand-written-dist + runtime-symlink foundation was sound.
Hydration handled as additive fixes (add client hydration, then improve it) rather than a foundational render-pipeline refactor.
Declares completion without ever confirming a passing test count (results file never produced); no re-verification of dependents after the pivots, so no coherent architecture is demonstrably reached.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent twice revises an approach when reality contradicts it — the dependency/packaging scheme (91-127) and the RSC integration (133-143, with explicit weighing) — matching anchor 5's 'recognizes an approach is wrong and reworks that subsystem.' It falls short of 8 because the RSC pivot chooses a workaround that bypasses the foundation rather than correctly wiring it, much of the middle is undifferentiated local patching of the runtime-symlink foundation (151-213), and it never re-verifies dependents or reaches a green suite (263-267). Net behavior lands between the 5 and 8 anchors, closer to 5.

dimensions.name: Resisting overfit to the visible suite

evidence.note: Studied Next.js base-server.ts and route-matcher-providers to implement general file-system routing that scans app/ and pages/ directories, rather than mapping specific fixture URLs — a general-contract approach.

Built all next/* shims (navigation, headers, cache, server, router, etc.) against the next-shims.d.ts type signatures with 'proper implementations', not per-test stubs, implementing actual module semantics.

Framing consistently 'pass all 335 tests' / 'comprehensive implementation'; no mention anywhere of the 373 hidden tests or that the visible suite is only a sample — no explicit visible-vs-hidden gap reasoning.
Plan to study upstream route resolution/SSR/middleware and implement proper routing generically, confirming a semantics-first (not fixture-fitting) orientation even mid-way.

Later work centered on general behaviors (hydration markers React expects, headers/cookies context passing) driven by reference contract, not hardcoding fixture text; no overfit shortcuts observed even under time pressure.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent implemented actual Next.js semantics inferred from the vendored source and shim types — file-system routing, general shims, config-driven redirects — with no observed hardcoding or fixture special-casing, placing it clearly above anchor 3. But it never articulated the visible-vs-hidden test gap or that the suite is a sample not the target, and did no stress-testing beyond the visible behaviors, so it falls short of anchors 8 and 10. This matches the level-5 description of general-contract implementation without explicit anti-overfit reasoning.

rubric.task_read: This is a maximally long-horizon, high-complexity build: reimplement the core of Next.js (CLI, Pages + App routers, SSR, SSG, `use cache`, server actions, middleware, `after()`, client hooks, and a Vite plugin that shims `next/*`) as a single `vinext` package on Vite's plugin API, with no internet and only vendored source to learn from. Difficulty comes from the sheer surface area, tightly-coupled subsystems, contracts that must be reverse-engineered from vendored Next.js/Vite source and fixture `next-shims.d.ts`, and a moving target (335 visible → 373 hidden tests). A skilled practitioner would invest heavily and continuously in every meta-work faculty; ceremony risk is low, thrash-and-lose-the-plot risk is very high.

dimensions.name: Reference mining & contract inference
dimensions.description: Studying vendored Vite/Next.js source and fixture type shims to understand the Vite plugin API and the exact `next/*` contracts before and while implementing, rather than guessing framework semantics.
dimensions.why_it_matters: There is no internet; correct behavior lives entirely in the vendored source and the fixtures' `next-shims.d.ts`. Guessing Next.js semantics or the Vite plugin lifecycle guarantees rework across a huge surface.

anchors.0: Starts coding shims/routing from memory of Next.js without opening any reference or fixture file.
anchors.3: Skims one or two reference files or a fixture shim, then proceeds mostly on assumption; contracts are inferred loosely.
anchors.5: Reads the relevant Vite plugin API surface and the fixture `next-shims.d.ts` for the subsystem currently being built; grounds each `next/*` shim in an actual type signature.
anchors.8: Systematically maps the vendored Next.js source and Vite plugin hooks to the required subsystems, extracts precise contracts from every fixture shim, and re-consults source when behavior is ambiguous rather than guessing; notes non-obvious semantics (e.g. RSC boundaries, cache keys, action serialization).
anchors.10: Sustained, targeted research throughout the build: continuously cross-references upstream source to resolve edge-case semantics as they surface, distinguishes what the fixtures actually require from full Next.js behavior, and builds an accurate mental/written model of how routing, RSC, and module resolution interlock — visibly preventing whole classes of rework.

dimensions.name: Subsystem decomposition & sequencing
dimensions.description: Breaking the framework into ordered, independently-verifiable subsystems (module shim/resolution, dev server, routing, SSR, SSG, caching, actions, CLI/build) with a dependency-aware sequence and done-criteria per milestone.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The subsystems are tightly coupled and one package must ship all of them; without dependency-aware sequencing and explicit milestones the agent will build in an order that forces constant backtracking and never reaches a testable state.

anchors.0: Treats the whole thing as one undifferentiated coding push; no ordering or sub-goals.
anchors.3: A flat, generic list mirroring the requirement bullets, with no dependency ordering or done-criteria.
anchors.5: Identifies the major subsystems and picks a sensible order (e.g. resolution/plugin before routing before SSR/SSG), with a rough notion of when each is 'done'.
anchors.8: Dependency-aware milestone plan that sequences a minimal end-to-end path (one route rendering under dev) before layering features, each milestone tied to concrete fixtures/tests that prove it, and revisited as the build reveals coupling.
anchors.10: A living decomposition that establishes a thin vertical slice early, orders remaining subsystems to maximize how soon tests can gate progress, explicitly manages interfaces between subsystems so they compose, and re-plans milestone boundaries as integration realities emerge — never losing the through-line across the long horizon.

dimensions.name: Test-driven verification design
dimensions.description: Deliberately using and extending the Playwright suite and fixture apps as checks — running targeted subsets per subsystem, building smaller probes, and verifying behavior beyond just 'it compiles'.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The 335-test suite is the ground truth, but it is slow and coarse; verifying each subsystem needs faster, targeted checks and running the right fixtures, or the agent flies blind between rare full-suite runs.

anchors.0: Never runs the test suite or the fixture apps; assumes correctness from the code alone.
anchors.3: Runs the full suite occasionally as a pass/fail oracle with no targeted or intermediate verification.
anchors.5: Runs relevant test subsets / individual fixtures for the subsystem in progress and uses failures to guide fixes; verifies dev and build paths work.
anchors.8: Designs a verification loop: fast targeted checks per subsystem, standing up fixtures manually to observe SSR/SSG/action behavior, and using the suite as a regression gate rather than a debugger; confirms both `dev` and the production `build`/`start` paths.
anchors.10: Builds a deliberate, layered verification strategy — minimal reproductions for hard subsystems (RSC, caching, actions), interprets test failures by root cause rather than symptom, and actively probes behaviors the visible suite may under-cover, treating passing tests as necessary-not-sufficient evidence of a faithful reimplementation.

dimensions.name: Progress & pass-rate tracking across subsystems
dimensions.description: Maintaining an accurate, current picture of which subsystems/tests pass vs. remain, and detecting circular debugging or regressions across a very large surface.
dimensions.why_it_matters: With hundreds of tests and many interdependent subsystems over a long horizon, it is easy to fix one area while regressing another, or to loop on the same failure; an accurate done-vs-remaining picture is what sustains forward motion.

anchors.0: No tracking of what passes or what is left; works reactively with no sense of overall state.
anchors.3: Vague recollection of progress; notices only whatever failure is in front of it.
anchors.5: Tracks pass counts / which subsystems are done and which are pending, and re-checks after changes to catch obvious regressions.
anchors.8: Maintains a structured, updated view of pass-rate by area, watches for regressions when touching shared code, and recognizes when it is looping on one failure and steps back rather than retrying blindly.
anchors.10: Continuously reconciles a precise model of done-vs-remaining against real test evidence across the whole surface, catches subtle cross-subsystem regressions early, quantifies progress toward the full suite, and reallocates effort to the highest-leverage remaining failures rather than drifting.

dimensions.name: Design revision under divergence
dimensions.description: Revising the architecture or approach (module resolution scheme, rendering pipeline, cache/action wiring) when reality — failing tests or discovered semantics — contradicts the initial design, rather than patching around a flawed foundation.
dimensions.why_it_matters: Early architectural choices (how `next/*` is intercepted, how RSC/SSR is wired into Vite) will be partly wrong; the agent must be willing to refactor the foundation instead of piling hacks that make later subsystems impossible.

anchors.0: Barrels ahead on the original approach even as failures accumulate; only adds patches.
anchors.3: Makes local fixes when something breaks but never revisits an underlying design decision even when it is clearly the cause.
anchors.5: Recognizes when an approach is wrong and reworks that subsystem, absorbing the cost rather than hacking around it.
anchors.8: Detects when a foundational choice (resolution, render pipeline) is blocking multiple subsystems and refactors it deliberately, updating the plan and re-verifying dependents afterward.
anchors.10: Treats falsified assumptions as signals to rethink the design cleanly, weighs refactor-vs-workaround explicitly, executes foundational pivots without losing already-passing behavior, and emerges with a more coherent architecture — demonstrating sustained self-correction across the horizon.

dimensions.name: Resisting overfit to the visible suite
dimensions.description: Implementing faithful, general framework behavior rather than special-casing the 335 visible tests, given explicit notice that 373 hidden tests over the same behavior will judge the work.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The spec openly states the final grade uses a larger hidden suite covering the same behaviors; an agent that hard-codes to visible fixtures will pass locally and fail the real metric, so recognizing and countering this gap is a distinct, decisive meta-work demand.

anchors.0: Hard-codes outputs or narrowly special-cases the visible fixtures/tests to turn them green.
anchors.3: Mostly general but reaches for a fixture-specific shortcut when a behavior is hard, without noting the risk.
anchors.5: Implements the actual semantics for each behavior rather than test-specific hacks, aware the suite is a sample not the target.
anchors.8: Explicitly reasons about the visible-vs-hidden gap, generalizes each subsystem to the real Next.js contract from the reference, and avoids overfitting even under schedule pressure.
anchors.10: Systematically implements to the general contract inferred from upstream source and shim types, stress-tests behaviors beyond what the visible tests exercise to expose overfit, and can articulate why the implementation should hold on unseen cases of the same behavior.
